newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Opposition, union heap pressure on S.Korea's Kim.
newsitem.headline: Opposition, union heap pressure on S.Korea's Kim.

text.p: In a dramatic challenge, South Korea's opposition parties on Wednesday rejected President Kim Young-sam's offer to reopen debate on a new labour law and the nation's top strike leader led a protest march through Seoul.

Park Sun-sook of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics said a meeting of officials from her party and the United Liberal Democratic Party decided any debate in parliament would be held only on condition the law was first revoked.
Separately, union leader Kwon Young-kil left Myongdong Cathedral to lead 4,000 workers in a noisy protest march against the law after workers responded only partially to a strike call.

For the first time since the law was rammed through parliament on December 26, Kwon and several deputies of the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions left the church where they had sought sanctuary from arrest.

The opposition's announcement and the one-hour march came just a day after a major reversal by President Kim, who agreed to reopen parliamentary debate on the law, which allows companies to sack workers and replace strikers.

As part of his climbdown, Kim said during a meeting with opposition leaders he would order officials to suspend arrest warrants served on Kwon and his deputies for organising more than three weeks of wildcat strikes.
But Park from the National Congress said: "Any debate in parliament must be made on the condition that the law is made null and void."
Kim, who argues the law would free up the labour market and trim company costs as well as boost competitiveness, has said dumping the legislation would go against the constitution.
Up until his stunning about-face, he had refused even to meet opposition leaders to discuss the law.
His sudden reversal on Tuesday followed a decision by the confederation to call off indefinite work stoppages and limit industrial action to one day each week on Wednesdays.
Analysts said the opposition was capitalising on Kim's blunder in a presidential election year of allowing his ruling New Korea Party to railroad the bill through parliament.
During Tuesday's meeting, Kim conceded the law had caused public anxiety and damaged the economy.
Analysts have said Kim was also bowing to public criticism over the forced passage of the law, with many commentators comparing his tactics to those of previous military rulers.
Kwon, wearing a red headband inscribed with the Korean word for "fight", remained silent as marchers chanted "repeal the evil law" and "we need a new labour law".
There were no clashes with scores of riot police who kept a close watch on the protesters as they marched near the church.
One bystander rushed out and embraced Kwon, a former Paris-based correspondent for a South Korean newspaper, before lifting him in the air.

Kwon was eventually stopped by police ostensibly because the crowd carried a large banner, which they did not report to police before getting permission for the march. All street protests require prior approval from the authorities.
There were no reports of violence.
Kwon later returned to the cathedral, where the group has pitched a makeshift tent to house its strike headquarters.
Police have withdrawn a security cordon from the church following Kim's order to suspend the arrest warrants.
The confederation has insisted the government scrap the law before it takes affect on March 1 and come up with a new bill.
The Labour Ministry said 68,500 workers from the country's 12-million strong workforce observed the strike call. It said this was mainly confined to the automobile industry.
The confederation said about 140,000 workers downed tools.
In the southeast city of Ulsan, a Reuters correspondent said the vast Hyundai Motor Co complex was paralysed. Giant robots lay idle and night shift workers had not turned up.
Union official Yoon Jong-o said 20,000 out of the 35,000 automaker's workers had observed the strike call.
"Partially changing the law doesn't solve the problem. We need to start all over again," he said.
A union official from the Ulsan-based Hyundai Heavy Industries, the nation's largest shipyard, said only 210 workers had joined the stoppages.
Union members at automaker Kia Motors, located just outside Seoul, held partial strikes in the afternoon.
